Since \(m\) is even, \(a_n\equiv1\pmod{n+1}\), so \(\gcd(a_n,b_n)=1\) and no reduction ever occurs. Hence \(b_n\to\infty\) and all terms are distinct, so the sequence is not eventually periodic.

**Odd \(m\) work.** Write \(q_n=a_n/b_n\) in lowest terms. Because \(m\) is odd, \(a_2\equiv a_1+b_1\pmod2\) is odd, and thereafter every numerator stays odd. The reduction factor is
\[
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1}+mb_{n-1},\,b_{n-1}+1)=\gcd(a_{n-1}-m,\,b_{n-1}+1).
\]
For \(n\ge2\): if \(b_{n-1}\) is odd then \(b_{n-1}+1\) and \(a_{n-1}-m\) are even, so \(g_n\ge2\) and \(b_n\le(b_{n-1}+1)/2\); if \(b_{n-1}\) is even then \(b_n\mid b_{n-1}+1\) gives \(b_n\le b_{n-1}+1\) (odd), whence \(b_{n+1}\le(b_{n-1}+2)/2\). Thus whenever \(b_{n-1}\ge3\), we have \(b_{n+1}<b_{n-1}\); the denominators are therefore bounded.

With denominators bounded by \(B\), the recurrence \(q_{n+1}=b_n(q_n+m)/(b_n+1)\) implies that if \(q_n>mB\) then \(q_{n+1}<q_n\), while otherwise \(q_{n+1}\le B(mB+m)\). Hence numerators are also bounded, leaving only finitely many possible reduced fractions. Every orbit must therefore eventually repeat, i.e. be eventually periodic.

Write \(q_n=a_n/b_n\) in lowest terms. Then
\[
b_n=\frac{b_{n-1}+1}{d_n},\qquad d_n=\gcd(b_{n-1}+1,\;a_{n-1}+mb_{n-1})=\gcd(b_{n-1}+1,\;a_{n-1}-m).
\]

**Even \(m\) fails.** Take \(u=1\). Induction gives
\[
q_n=\frac{\frac{m}{2}n(n-1)+1}{n},
\]
and since \(m/2\in\mathbb Z\) the numerator is \(\equiv1\pmod n\); hence the fraction is reduced and \(b_n=n\to\infty\). So the sequence is not eventually periodic.

**Odd \(m\) works.** Assume \(m\) is odd. From the gcd formula:
- if \(b\) is even, then \(a\) is odd, \(d\) is odd, so the next denominator is odd and the next numerator is odd;
- if \(b\) and \(a\) are odd, then \(b+1\) and \(a-m\) are even, so \(d\) is even and the next denominator is at most \((b+1)/2\);
- if \(b\) is odd and \(a\) is even, then \(a-m\) is odd, so \(d\) is odd and the next denominator is even.

Hence whenever \(b\ge5\), after at most three steps the denominator strictly decreases; consequently the denominators become bounded (in fact eventually \(\le5\)).

Once denominators are bounded, say by \(B\), if \(a>mB^2\) then \(a>mb^2\) and the next unreduced value \((a+mb)/(b+1)\) is strictly smaller than \(a/b\). A strictly decreasing sequence of positive rationals whose denominators divide \(\mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,B)\) must terminate, so eventually \(a\le mB^2\). Thus only finitely many reduced pairs \((a,b)\) occur, and the sequence is eventually periodic.

Therefore the required \(m\) are exactly the odd positive integers.
